title: An Analysis on Collegiate Athletes: Injuries and Performance

Data Source:
This analysis uses the Athlete Injury and Performance dataset by [Ziya], obtained from Kaggle and licensed under CC0: Public Domain.
Source: Athlete Injury and Performance Dataset

title: An Analysis on Collegiate Athletes: Injuries and Performance
text:
Intro
The bane of any athlete’s existence is: Injury.
You can try to escape from it; do your stretching, conditioning, strengthening, but it’ll always catch up to you in some way unexpectedly. The most you can do is prime the body to try to prevent injuries.
It’s a lot easier to get injured as you get older. That’s why, when you’re young, you think you’re invincible. So, it should make sense that people aged 18-25 at their athletic peak should be the least injury-prone, right? Wrong. The higher level in competitive sports you go, the more risk of injury there is. Thus, through this dataset, we will try to analyze How do training load, recovery, and fatigue differ between injured and healthy collegiate athletes?

This dataset is comprised of 200 collegiate basektball players of both genders and of varying heights, weights and positions. We can see that out of the 200 players, 93% of the players are healthy but 7% of them are injured.
Although 7% might not seem like a lot, it’s easier to put it into perspective if you consider how they should be in their peak, they get premium training, nutrition, etc.

From this summary alone we can see the clearer story between the healthy and the injured. On average, the injured trains more intensely, trains over 2 hours more, takes less recovery days, have much higher fatigue, their ACL risk is almost double and their load balance is lower too. These are all telltale signs that someone is about to be injured or is already injured.

title: An Analysis on Collegiate Athletes: Injuries and Performance
text:
Focusing on fatigue

fatigue_summary = athletes.groupby('Injury_Indicator')['Fatigue_Score'].mean()

fatigue_summary.plot(kind="bar")

plt.xlabel("Injury status")
plt.ylabel("Average fatigue score")
plt.title("Average Fatigue Score by Injury Status")
plt.xticks([0, 1], ["Healthy", "Injury"], rotation=0)
plt.yticks(range(11))

plt.show()








Humans have drive and grit, and there’s been a long-standing narrative that we have to push past our limits in order to accomplish something. That’s only true to an extent and we have to be able to manage that to make sure nothing breaks; figuratively and literally speaking.
Fatigue is one of the most basic indicators that tell us that our bodies need rest. The more fatigue the body experiences, the more at risk of injury too. Out of a 10-point scale, the fact that the injured athletes have a noticeably higher score on fatigue is concering. The healthy athletes maintain a baseline-level (suitable for athletes), at almost a score of 5. On the other hand, the injured is approaching a dangerous level with a score reaching almost an 8. With matches, practice, and additional training, fatigue is bound to keep amassing.

title: An Analysis on Collegiate Athletes: Injuries and Performance
text:
Does it affect Performance?

performance_summary = (
    athletes
    .groupby("Injury_Indicator")[
        ["Performance_Score", "Team_Contribution_Score"]
    ]
    .mean()
)

performance_summary.index = ["Healthy", "Injured"]

plt.ylabel("Average performance score")
plt.title("Average Performance Score by Injury Status")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.yticks(range(0,101,10))
plt.show()








With the habits of the injured players, we can see that it does make them perform better…marginally. The average performance score of a healthy player is 74.4, whereas the average performance score of an injured player is 75.7. Does overtraining make the performance score higher? Yes. Is it worth it? No.

title: An Analysis on Collegiate Athletes: Injuries and Performance
text:
Conclusion
Doing all that extra training, stressing the body to the brink of breaking, and hindering the body from resting only accounts for an almost obsolete increase in performance. The worst part is that tiny sliver of increase in performance may set the athlete back from training or even playing for extended periods of time. Then what? High risk, very low reward.
The lesson here is: even the greatest athletes get injured. The truly great athletes are the ones who are able to prolong their career by staying healthy.

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Data Source:
This analysis uses the Sports Training dataset by [VisionLangAI], obtained from Kaggle and licensed under CC BY 4.0.
Source: Sports Training

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Intro
There exist many methods and intensities that athletes can use to train. From a general perspective, most people think the same two things when it comes to training: Train hard, and Train smart.
But what does that really mean? Obviously, there are different sports and each sport has to train differrently. However, at the same time, each sport can take something away from another. Besides the sport, we need to consider the individuals playing the sport. Even if two players play the same sport, no two players will have the same psychological profile.
Through an analysis of this dataset, we will analyze training methods, adaptation types, intensity level and other factors to answer the question: Which psychological training methods are associated with better outcomes for athletes?

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Loading the Data

# Loading the data and inspecting
library(tidyverse)

sports <- read_csv('data/psych_training_sports.csv')
glimpse(sports)

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Examining the Training Methods

method_summary <- sports |>
    count(Training_Method, sort = TRUE) |>
    mutate(pct_total = n/sum(n) * 100)

method_summary

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  Training_Method             n pct_total
  <chr>                   <int>     <dbl>
1 Goal-setting            13059     26.1 
2 Self-talk               12934     25.9 
3 Mindfulness             12930     25.9 
4 Visualization            7033     14.1 
5 Cognitive Restructuring  4044      8.09


Here, we count all the available training methods recorded in this dataset and calculate their percentage. We can see that the most used training method for athletes is to set a goal for myself. However, this method is extremely comparable to self-talk and mindfulness as well, with all three hovering around 26% of the whole population. This makes sense as all three of these methods are what’s taught in life even away from sports. People are taught since adolescence to set a goal for themselves, to think over their actions, and be aware of their actions and the subsequent results. What’s interesting here, though, is that the lowest used method is cognitive restructuring: a method not very commonly heard of.

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Summarizing Effectiveness by Method

method_summary <- sports |>
    group_by(Training_Method) |>
    summarize(
        avg_motivation_gain = mean(Motivation_Gain, na.rm = TRUE),
        avg_confidence_gain = mean(Confidence_Gain, na.rm = TRUE),
        avg_stress_reduction = mean(Stress_Reduction_Percentage, na.rm = TRUE),
        avg_effectiveness = mean(Adaptation_Effectiveness_Score, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = 'drop'
    ) %>%
    left_join(method_summary, ., by='Training_Method')

method_summary |>
    print(width = Inf)

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Comparing Average Effectiveness

ggplot(
  method_summary,
  aes(
    y = reorder(Training_Method, avg_effectiveness),
    x = avg_effectiveness
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(avg_effectiveness, 2)),
    nudge_y = 0.15
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(11.8, 12.2)) +
  labs(
    x = "Average adaptation effectiveness score",
    y = "Training method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Average adaptation effectiveness score by psychological training method.





Even though some methods are preferred more than others, this figure above shows that the average adapatation effectiveness scores are very similar across all five training methods.
Self-talk method had the highest average score at about 12.06 while mindfulness had the lowest average score at about 11.96. This only produces a spread between the highest and lowest score at 0.10 points, which suggests that the training method alone isn’t very strongly associated with adaptation effectiveness in this dataset.

title: Psychological Effectiveness in Sports Training
text:
Relationship between Adherence and Effectiveness

tibble(
  measure = c("Pearson correlation", "Kendall's tau"),
  value = c(
    cor(
      sports$Training_Adherence_Rate,
      sports$Adaptation_Effectiveness_Score,
      use = "complete.obs",
      method = "pearson"
    ),
    cor(
      sports$Training_Adherence_Rate,
      sports$Adaptation_Effectiveness_Score,
      use = "complete.obs",
      method = "kendall"
    )
  )
)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  measure                value
  <chr>                  <dbl>
1 Pearson correlation -0.00923
2 Kendall's tau       -0.00474


With both Pearson’s correlation (-0.009) and Kendall’s tau (-0.005) nearing very closely to zero, we can see that there is essentially no linear nor monotonic association between adherence to training and the adaptation effectiveness score. This means that, within this dataset, higher adherence to training does not appear to correspond with higher or lower adaptation effectiveness.

title: About
text:
Life up until now
I grew up in Toronto and went to UWaterloo for undergrad like many other people. The summer after graduation was the only break I had before transitioning into the master’s program. Before that, I mainly worked in multiple internships within the fintech industry.

title: About
text:
Why Master’s?
It was actually my previous internships that first sparked my interest in data science. Working with a lot of financial data, it really drove home that data is the underlying factor of everything. I wanted to learn more about how I can create with data. Also, it wouldn’t hurt to try to experience a new life in Vancouver.

title: About

On a normal day, I’d probably jump at any opportunity to play volleyball. However, it’s not sustainable to play every day so I end up working out more often. Otherwise, my life is simple: a black iced coffee, good food, good company and the occasional scenic nature walk.
